label: Sayings LXXXIV–CIX
paragraphs: LXXXIV. For my part, may death find me attending to nothing but my own will, so that it may be free of passion, unhindered, uncompelled, free. This is what I want to be found doing, so that I can say to God, "Did I break your commands? Did I use the means you gave me for other ends? Did I misuse my senses, or my preconceptions? Did I ever accuse you? Did I find fault with the way you govern? I was sick when you wished it; so were others, but I was willing. I became poor because you wished it, but gladly. I held no office, because you did not wish it; I never desired office. Did you ever see me gloomier on that account? Did I not always come before you with a cheerful face, ready for whatever you ordered, whatever sign you gave? Now you want me to leave the festival. I go. I am wholly grateful to you that you thought me worthy to share the festival with you, and to see your works, and to understand with you the way you govern." May death find me thinking these things, writing these things, reading these things.

LXXXV. Does it seem nothing to you never to accuse anyone, God or man; never to blame anyone; always to carry the same face going out and coming in? These were the things Socrates knew, and yet he never said that he knew or taught anything. Which of you, then, has this aim? For if you had it, you would be glad to be sick, and to go hungry, and to die.

LXXXVI. And how were we born to be? Free, noble, self-respecting. For what other animal blushes? What other takes in the impression of what is shameful? And put pleasure under these as a servant, an attendant, so that it may call out our eagerness and keep us at the works that are in keeping with nature.
LXXXVII. The material of the good and noble man is his own ruling faculty; the body is the material of the doctor and the trainer; the land is the farmer's material.

LXXXVIII. And who among us does not admire what Lycurgus the Spartan did? One of the citizens had blinded him in one eye, and the people handed the young man over to him to punish as he wished. He did not punish him. He educated him, made a good man of him, and brought him into the theater. And when the Spartans were amazed, he said, "I received this man from you insolent and violent. I give him back to you reasonable and a good citizen."

LXXXIX. The banker is not allowed to reject Caesar's coin, nor is the man who sells vegetables; if you show it, he must hand over what it buys, whether he wants to or not. It is the same with the soul. The good, as soon as it appears, draws the soul toward itself; evil drives it away. A soul will never reject a clear impression of good, any more than a man will reject Caesar's coin. On this hangs every movement of man and of God.

XC. When someone asked what common sense is, he said: Just as we might call a kind of hearing common when it only tells sounds apart, while the kind that tells musical notes apart is no longer common but a matter of art, so there are certain things that men who are not altogether warped see by the starting points common to all. That state of mind is called common sense.

XCI. Do you know how to judge? Then make us want to be like you, as Socrates made men want to be like him. "Do this; do not do that; or I will throw you into prison": that is no longer ruling us as rational beings. Say instead, "Do this as Zeus has ordered; and if you do not, you will be penalized, you will be harmed." What harm? No other than this: not doing what you should. You will destroy the trustworthy man in you, the self-respecting man, the decent man. Look for no greater harms than these.

XCII. "His son is dead." What happened? His son is dead. Nothing else? Nothing. "The ship was lost." What happened? The ship was lost. "He was taken off to prison." What happened? He was taken off to prison. But "he has fared badly": that each man adds from himself. "But Zeus does not do right in this." Why? Because he made you able to endure, because he made you great of soul, because he took away from these things the power to be evils, because you can be happy while suffering them, because he opened the door for you whenever things do not suit you? Man, go out, and do not complain.

XCIII. You are sailing to Rome now to become patron of the people of Cnossus; it is not enough for you to stay at home with the honors you had; you want something greater and more conspicuous. When did you ever sail like this to examine your own judgments and, if you had a bad one, to throw it out? Whom have you ever visited for that purpose? What time have you set aside for it, what part of your life? Go over the years of your life, by yourself if you are ashamed to do it before me. When you were a boy, did you examine your judgments? Did you not do what you did then just as you do everything now? And when you were a youth and went to hear the teachers of rhetoric and practiced speaking yourself, what did you imagine you lacked? And when you were a young man and had entered public life, and were pleading cases yourself and making a name, who still seemed your equal? And when would you have put up with being examined by anyone, to show that your judgments were bad? What, then, do you want me to say to you? "Help me in this business." I have no teachings for that. And if that is what you came to me for, you have not come to me as to a philosopher, but as to a man who sells vegetables, or a shoemaker. "What do philosophers have teachings for, then?" For this: whatever happens, to keep our ruling faculty in keeping with nature and to go on so. Does that seem a small thing to you? "No, the greatest." What then? Does it need only a little time? Can it be picked up in passing? If you can, pick it up. Then you will say, "I met Epictetus." Yes, as you would meet a stone or a statue. For you saw me, and nothing more. A man meets a man, as a man, when he learns his judgments and in turn shows his own. Learn my judgments; show me yours; and then say you have met me. Let us test each other. If I have a bad judgment, take it away; if you have one, bring it out. That is what it is to meet a philosopher. But no. "We are passing through, and while we are hiring the ship we can see Epictetus too. Let us see what he has to say." Then, as you leave: "Epictetus was nothing. His grammar was bad and his speech was foreign." For what else do you come in to judge?

XCIV. You, however much you own, need something else: whether you like it or not, you are poorer than I am. "What do I need, then?" What you do not have: steadiness, a mind in keeping with nature, freedom from trouble. Patron or no patron, what do I care? You care. I am richer than you. I am not anxious about what Caesar will think of me; I flatter no one for that. This is what I have in place of your silver plate and your gold plate. You have vessels of gold, but your reason is of clay, and your judgments, your assents, your impulses, your desires.

XCV. Everything you have seems small to you; everything I have seems great to me. Your desire is never filled; mine is filled already. The same thing happens to children who put a hand into a narrow-necked jar to take out figs and nuts. If a child fills his hand, he cannot get it out, and then he cries. Let a few of them go and you will get it out. You too, let your desire go. Do not want many things, and you will get what you want.
XCVI. Pittacus, wronged by a man he had the power to punish, let him go, saying, "Forgiveness is better than revenge." The one belongs to a gentle nature, the other to a savage one.

XCVII. "My brother ought not to have treated me this way." No; but that is for him to see to. However he treats me, I will deal with him as I should. For this is mine, and that is another's; this no one can hinder, and that can be hindered.

XCVIII. But all the same a man must prepare himself for this too: to be able to be enough for himself, to be able to keep his own company. As Zeus keeps company with himself, and is at rest in himself, and reflects on what his own governance is like, and is occupied with thoughts that suit him, so we too should be able to talk with ourselves, to have no need of others, not to be at a loss for something to do. We should turn our minds to the divine governance and to our own relationship to everything else; look at how we used to stand toward the things that happen and how we stand now; what the things are that still weigh on us; how these too may be cured, how they may be removed; and if any of this needs working out, work it out as its own reason requires.

XCIX. A man who mixes often with certain people, for talk or for dinner parties or simply to share their life, must either become like them or bring them over to his own ways. For if you put a dead coal beside a burning one, either it will put the other out or the other will set it alight. Since the danger is so great, we must be careful about entering into such dealings with laymen, remembering that a man who rubs against someone covered in soot cannot help getting some of the soot on himself. For what will you do if he talks about gladiators, about horses, about athletes, or, what is worse still, about people: "So-and-so is bad, so-and-so is good; this was well done, that was badly done"? Or if he mocks, or jokes, or shows ill nature? Has any of you the preparation a lyre player has when he takes up the lyre, so that as soon as he touches the strings he knows which are out of tune, and tunes the instrument? Or the power Socrates had, so that in every kind of company he led those who were with him over to his own side? Where would you get that from? No; you are bound to be carried about by the laymen. Why then are they stronger than you? Because they say their rotten things out of their judgments, and you say your fine things from the lips only. That is why what you say is slack and dead, and why it turns the stomach to hear your exhortations and your poor virtue, which you chatter about up and down. So the laymen beat you. For everywhere judgment is strong; judgment is invincible.

C. And for the rest, whatever is applied to the body by those who exercise it, if it leans in some way toward desire and aversion, may also count as training. But if it is for display, it is the mark of a man who has turned outward and is hunting for something else, and looking for spectators to say, "What a great man!" That is why Apollonius was right to say, "When you want to train for your own sake, then sometime when you are thirsty in the heat, take a mouthful of cold water, and spit it out, and tell no one."

CI. Practice sometimes living like a sick man, so that someday you may live like a healthy one. Go without food; drink water. Keep away from desire altogether for a time, so that someday you may also desire with good reason.

CII. You want to do them good? Show them in your own person what kind of men philosophy makes, and stop talking nonsense. When you eat, do good to those who eat with you; when you drink, to those who drink with you. By giving way to everyone, making room for them, putting up with them: do them good in that way, and do not spit your own phlegm over them.

CIII. As bad tragic singers cannot sing alone, but only with many others, so some people cannot walk alone. Man, if you are anyone, walk alone too, and talk to yourself, and do not hide in the chorus. Let yourself be mocked for once; look around you; give yourself a shake, so that you may know who you are.

CIV. "I want to win at Olympia." But look at what comes before it and what follows, and then, if it is to your advantage, put your hand to the work. You must keep discipline, eat by rule, stay away from pastries, train under compulsion at a fixed hour, in heat, in cold. You must not drink cold water, or wine whenever you happen to. In a word, you must hand yourself over to your trainer as you would to a doctor. Then in the contest you must dig in against your opponent, sometimes put out a wrist, twist an ankle, swallow a great deal of sand, take a whipping; and after all this, sometimes be beaten. When you have reckoned all this up, if you still want to, go and be an athlete. If not, know that you will be behaving like children, who play at athletes one moment and gladiators the next, then blow a trumpet, then act a tragedy, whatever they have seen and admired. So you too are an athlete now, then a gladiator, then a philosopher, then an orator, and nothing with your whole soul. Like an ape you imitate whatever you see, and one thing after another pleases you, but what you are used to displeases you. For you did not come to anything after looking into it, or after going all round the matter and testing it, but at random and with a cold desire. Man, consider first what the thing is, and then your own nature, what you can carry. If you would be a wrestler, look at your shoulders, your thighs, your back. For different men are born for different things. Do you think you can do what you do now and be a philosopher? Do you think you can eat the same way, drink the same way, be angry in the same way, be discontented in the same way? You must stay awake, you must work hard, you must overcome certain desires, leave your own people, be looked down on by a slave boy, be laughed at by those you meet, come off worse in everything, in office, in honor, in court. When you have looked hard at all this, come to it if you think fit, if you are willing to exchange these things for freedom from passion, freedom, and peace of mind.
CV. For in music the unmusical man is a child; in letters, the unlettered; in life, the uneducated.

CVI. "Can any good be got from these people, then?" From everyone. "Even from the man who abuses me?" What good does his sparring partner do an athlete? The greatest. And this man becomes my sparring partner: he trains my patience, my freedom from anger, my gentleness. But no. The man who takes hold of my neck and puts my back and shoulders in shape does me good, and the trainer is right to say, "Lift the pestle with both hands," and the heavier it is, the more good it does me; but if someone trains me to be free from anger, he does me no good? That is what it is not to know how to get good from people. A bad neighbor? Bad for himself, but good for me: he trains my good temper and my fairness. A bad father? Bad for himself, but good for me. This is the wand of Hermes. "Touch whatever you like," they say, "and it will turn to gold." No; but bring whatever you like and I will make it good. Bring sickness, bring death, bring poverty, bring abuse, bring a trial for my life: by the wand of Hermes all these will become a benefit.

CVII. So until these fine opinions are fixed fast in you, and you have gained some power to keep yourselves safe, I advise you to be careful about going down among laymen. Otherwise whatever you write down in the school will melt away day by day like wax in the sun. So take yourselves off somewhere far from the sun, as long as your opinions are made of wax.

CVIII. These things must be approached in another way. The matter is great, it is a mystery, not a thing given at random or to just anyone. Perhaps even being wise is not enough for taking care of the young. There must also be a certain readiness and fitness for it, and, by Zeus, a certain kind of body, and above all God must advise a man to take up this post, as he advised Socrates to take the post of examining and refuting, Diogenes that of the king who rebukes, Zeno that of teaching and laying down doctrine. But you open a doctor's office with nothing but medicines; where or how they are applied you neither know nor have troubled to find out.

CIX. But if the teachings charm you, sit and turn them over by yourself. Never call yourself a philosopher, and do not put up with anyone else who calls you one. Say, "He is mistaken. For I do not desire differently than before, or feel impulses toward other things, or assent to other things; in the use of impressions I have not changed at all from my former state."

divergences.phrase: πηρωθεὶς γὰρ ὑπό τινος τῶν πολιτῶν τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν τὸν ἕτερον
divergences.older: "A young citizen had put out his eye" (Crossley)
divergences.lectio: "One of the citizens had blinded him in one eye"
divergences.note: Crossley's "his" can be read either way; the Greek is plain that Lycurgus lost the eye and the young man was handed to him for punishment. The closing pair ἐπιεικῆ καὶ δημοτικόν is "reasonable and a good citizen" (literally "a man of the people"), not Crossley's "in his right mind and fit to serve his country". The passage is fragment 5 in Schenkl, from Stobaeus, headed "From Rufus, out of Epictetus on friendship".

divergences.older: "at length think; look around thee; bestir thyself" (Crossley, reading σκέψαι)
divergences.lectio: "Let yourself be mocked for once; look around you; give yourself a shake"
divergences.note: Schenkl keeps the manuscript's σκώφθητι, "be jeered at": the man who leaves the chorus and walks alone will be laughed at, and should let it happen. Crossley translated an old correction to "consider".

divergences.lectio: Crossley's saying put into current English
divergences.note: The Pittacus saying is one of the fragments Schweighäuser took from the anthologies. Schenkl does not print it and no Greek was to hand (it is Schweighäuser's fragment 68), so this paragraph alone in the section is made from Crossley's English, checked against George Long's independent version (1877), which agrees. It needs the Greek before the edition is called ready.
